Lecture/Lab Hours: 2.0 lecture  Grades: Eligible Grades: A-F,PR,WP,WF,WN,FN,AU,I  Learning Outcomes:  Students will be able to demonstrate knowledge of the principles underlying the various parameters that can be adjusted on thermal and electro-therapeutic equipment.Students will be able to analyze how adjusting the parameter settings on a given piece of thermal or electro-therapeutic equipment will affect the output of the equipment and the response of the patient.Students will be able to describe the physiological effects of thermal agents on various tissues and differentiate the responses of healthy and impaired tissues.Students will be able to state the indications and contra-indications of both thermal and electro-therapeutic physical agents in clinical care.Students will be able to describe how different physical agents can affect tissue repair and apply this knowledge to various patient problems.Students will be able to describe the mechanisms underlying the role of physical agents in pain modulation.Students will be able to analyze safety issues associated with both thermal and electro-therapeutic physical agents.Students will be able to safely apply all of the physical agents utilized in this course.Students will be able to determine the most appropriate physical agent to utilize for a given case so as to maximize effectiveness of therapeutic interventions.Students will be able to determine how to appropriately operate and safely apply a given piece of therapeutic equipment.Students will be able to describe the basic principles, and demonstrate knowledge of appropriate applications, of compression in patient management.Students will be able to apply knowledge of the pathophysiological causes of lymphedema to the appropriate use of common techniques for the treatment of lymphedema.Students will be able to use existing scientific literature to guide treatment of a given patient condition.

course_name: Pain Education and Management Fundamentals for the Physical Therapist
description: Navigates the learner towards a path of understanding and managing complex and chronic pain conditions. Pain processing models are reviewed, the influences and contributing factors to the pain experience are discussed, and the clinical skills needed to successfully manage pain-related disability and suffering are introduced. By the end of the course, learners are ready to apply this framework within clinical settings and be equipped to use thought challenging techniques to address unhelpful pain-coping strategies, motivational interviewing skills to promote self-efficacy, a graded activity approach for exercise progression, a graded exposure approach to reduce pain-related fear of movement, and mindfulness-informed teaching approach to cultivate body awareness and pain acceptance.   Requisites: PT 7041 and 7042   Repeat/Retake Information: May not be retaken.  Lecture/Lab Hours: 2.0 lecture  Grades: Eligible Grades: A-F,WP,WF,WN,FN,AU,I  Learning Outcomes:  Students will be able to apply a conceptual framework for understanding pain and disability for people with chronic pain.Students will be able to analyze pain assessment strategies for people with chronic pain.Students will be able to demonstrate treatment strategies for managing pain-related disability for people with chronic pain.Students will be able to outline management principles to patients with different complex pain conditions, such as fibromyalgia and neuropathic pain.Students will be able to compare the role of the physical therapist with other health professionals in managing patients with complex pain conditions.

Introduces students to the role of physical therapists in the evaluation and treatment of disorders of the integumentary system, with a focus on chronic wounds. Principles and techniques of patient management are presented throughout this course.   Requisites: PT 7651   Repeat/Retake Information: May not be retaken.  Lecture/Lab Hours: 2.0 lecture  Grades: Eligible Grades: A-F,PR,WP,WF,WN,FN,AU,I  Learning Outcomes:  Students will be able to describe the basic pathophysiology associated with non-healing chronic wounds of different etiologies.Students will be able to perform evaluative techniques for assessing wound severity.Students will be able to identify contributing factors (e.g., vascular vs. neuropathic) and interpret evaluative findings to provide accurate prognoses for wound healing.Students will be able to differentiate between chronic wounds with distinct pathologies (e.g., arterial vs. venous insufficiency).Students will be able to identify risk factors for given chronic wound types, including patient behaviors, and prescribe strategies for addressing these risks.Students will be able to select appropriate therapeutic interventions for treating chronic wounds based on the underlying mechanisms of action and prognoses associated with these interventions.Students will be able to outline the integumentary response to burn injury.Students will be able to prescribe effective rehabilitation strategies for patients with burns.Students will be able to screen for and identify common dermatological conditions in various patient populations.Students will be able to describe the role of physical agents in wound treatment based on wound type and severity.Students will be able to perform specific physical therapy interventions related to wound management.Students will be able to evaluate the clinical and scientific evidence supporting evaluation tools, interventions and outcome instruments related to integumentary patients.Students will be able to adapt interventions based on patient progress over a course of treatment.Students will be able to accurately document care of patients with integumentary disorders.Students will be able to adhere to practice standards and regulations related to wound care of patients and reimbursement for assessment and intervention.Students will be able to accurately diagnose wound etiology, develop and progress a holistic treatment plan and assess the effectiveness of this plan.

Discusses biological, histological and biomechanical principles of connective tissues, bone, and muscle as applied to physical examination and therapeutic exercise. There is presentation of medical imaging of the listed tissues as they appear on plane x-ray, MRI, fMRI, CT scan, PET/SPECT scan, and ultrasound as related to physical therapy practice. Basic principles of exercise prescription will be discussed to achieve optimal outcomes for the patient based on the pathology, biomechanical principles of tissues, impairment, and the desired level of performance.   Requisites: PT 7030   Repeat/Retake Information: May not be retaken.  Lecture/Lab Hours: 3.0 lecture, 3.0 laboratory  Grades: Eligible Grades: A-F,PR,WP,WF,WN,FN,AU,I  Learning Outcomes:  Students will describe bone, ligament, tendon, articular disk, and muscle histology.Students will describe the components of muscle architecture and apply the principles of muscle architecture to the force-length and force-velocity relationships in muscle.Students will describe the studies that led to and the implications of the length-tension and force-velocity relationships in muscle.Students will differentiate various body tissues on a given imaging system.Students will discuss basic engineering concepts and principles related to tissue material testing.Students will discuss the interaction of muscle and tendon in the production of movement.Students will explain the basic principles of muscle to adaptation that occur with increased and decreased load.Students will identify normal and pathological (selected conditions) presentations: normal bony and soft tissue anatomy, bone fractures, malalignment conditions, and selected pathological states of connective tissues, bone, and neurological tissues.Students will integrate the material properties and mechanics of muscle and other biological tissue to the development of a therapeutic exercise intervention.Students will recognize risks and benefits involved with a given imaging system including x-ray, fluoroscopy, contrast media usage, DEXA, and CT, MRI, and ultrasound.Students will state patient preparation for and the basic technical functioning of a given imaging system.Using simulated patient scenarios, students will analyze performance of therapeutic exercise to ensure it is executed correctly by either the physical therapist or the patient.Using simulated patient scenarios, students will choose the appropriate therapeutic exercise to meet the treatment goal.Using simulated patient scenarios, students will deliver appropriate dosage of exercise: intensity, duration, repetition, and frequency of exercise.Using simulated patient scenarios, students will demonstrate basic manual handling skills.Using simulated patient scenarios, students will position the patient and teach the patient to perform therapeutic exercise using verbal commands and demonstration.

course_name: Foundations of Tissue Mechanics for the Physical Therapist
description: The biological, histological, and biomechanical principles of connective tissues, nervous tissues, and muscular tissues and bone through the normal human growth, development, and aging cycle are covered. Tissue assessment and response to injury, typically used medications, and interventions are discussed. Further emphasis is placed on the principles of exercise prescription to achieve optimal outcomes for the patient based on the pathology, impairment, and the desired level of performance.   Requisites: PT 7011 and PT 7012   Repeat/Retake Information: May not be retaken.  Lecture/Lab Hours: 3.0 lecture  Grades: Eligible Grades: A-F,PR,WP,WF,WN,FN,AU,I  Learning Outcomes:  Students will be able to describe the histology of bone, ligament, tendon, articular cartilage, intra-articular disks, nerve, skeletal muscle, and intervertebral disks.Students will be able to explain the tensile, compressive, and shear properties of bone, ligament, tendon, articular cartilage, nerve, skeletal muscle, and cartilaginous disks.Students will be able to apply the material properties of biological tissue to the implementation of physical therapy treatments.Students will be able to describe the typical growth and development of soft tissue and bone throughout the normal life-span.Students will be able to summarize the effect of interventions such as medication (prescribed and OTC), nutrition, immobilization, and surgery on the mechanical properties of bone and soft tissue.Students will be able to develop a custom exercise program to meet the needs of a patient/client with abnormal bone and/or soft tissue throughout the lifespan.Students will be able to explain the utilization, benefits, and risks of joint arthroplasties.Students will be able to recognize the basic physiological events occurring in muscle contractionStudents will be able to describe the results of studies that led to the development of length-tension and force-velocity relationships in muscle, as well as their implications.Students will be able to describe the components of muscle architecture.Students will be able to describe the appropriate parameters for muscle stretching using evidence found in the literature.Students will be able to apply the characteristics of the passive properties of muscle to the evaluation of muscle flexibility and stretching.Students will be able to identify muscle and joint biomechanics in the production of torque.Students will be able to describe the interaction of muscle and tendon in the production of movement.Students will be able to describe the characteristics of muscle fiber types and muscle fiber adaptation as a result of therapeutic exercise.Students will be able to compare the various parameters of muscle strengthening and stretching in relation to the desired outcomes and the development of therapeutic exercises.Students will be able to differentiate between the various stages of tissue healing and the appropriate dosages of therapeutic exercise.

course_name: Clinical Application of Tissue Mechanics and Therapeutic Exercise for the Physical Therapist
description: The clinical application of therapeutic exercise principles will be applied based on the biological, histological, and biomechanical principles of connective tissue, nervous tissue, and skeletal muscle tissue. Emphasis will be placed on optimizing patient outcomes using evidence based procedures for healing tissues. Treatment considerations, such as patient’s age, pathology, biomechanical principles, activity level, and level of disability will help guide the underlying exercise applications.   Requisites: PT 7031 and PT 7032   Repeat/Retake Information: May not be retaken.  Lecture/Lab Hours: 2.0 lecture  Grades: Eligible Grades: A-F,PR,WP,WF,WN,FN,AU,I  Learning Outcomes:  Students will be able to demonstrate correct muscle stretching technique.Students will be able to apply the principles of muscle architecture to the force-length and force-velocity relationships in muscle when performing therapeutic exercise.Students will be able to apply the basic concepts of muscle strength to the production of muscle power and endurance during therapeutic exercise.Students will be able to apply the principles of strengthening, range of motion, and flexibility therapeutic exercises to patient cases.Students will be able to apply appropriate biomechanical principles while performing active, active-assist, and passive range of motion, and demonstrating correct technique based on a patient’s level of impairment.Students will be able to apply appropriate neural tissue biomechanical principles while performing neural tension techniques in the upper and lower extremities.Students will be able to apply appropriate biomechanical principles while performing various strengthening modalities, such as isometric, isotonic, isokinetic, open kinetic chain and closed kinetic chain activities.Students will be able to develop and perform appropriate therapeutic interventions based on tissue healing principles.

Focuses on orthopedic examination and treatment of the upper quarter of the musculoskeletal system, as well as a brief introduction to the cervical spine. Designed around the understanding of and subsequent application of the anatomy, mechanics, pathomechanics, pathology, surgical intervention, and rehabilitation to physical therapy case studies involving the upper quarter.  Content includes orthopedic evaluation skills, advanced skill development in special tests, introduction to manual therapy of the extremities, and development of appropriate exercise programs.   Requisites: PT 7700   Repeat/Retake Information: May not be retaken.  Lecture/Lab Hours: 2.0 lecture, 3.0 laboratory  Grades: Eligible Grades: A-F,PR,WP,WF,WN,FN,AU,I  Learning Outcomes:  In conjunction with the patient, family, payers, and other professionals, students will establish, implement, and manage a physical therapy treatment plan of care based upon the patient evaluation and knowledge of available treatment methods.The student will analyze the impact of normal and abnormal arthrokinematics, muscle length/strength and capsule properties on the function of the upper quarter.The student will analyze the pathological conditions presented in class and clinical case studies in terms of the etiology, mechanism of injury, surgical procedure, common signs and symptoms, resultant deformities, and the prognosis for recovery.The student will apply relevant biological and biomechanical characteristics of extremity tissues to functional and clinical situations.The student will consistently and critically evaluate sources of information related to physical therapy practice and research and apply knowledge from these sources in a scientific manner and to appropriate populations.The student will consistently integrate the best evidence for practice from sources of information with clinical judgment and patient/client values to determine the best care for a patient/client.The student will delegate responsibilities for certain treatments to physical therapy assistants, and other support personnel as appropriate.The student will describe, in detail, the normal and abnormal arthrokinematics, muscle length/strength, and capsular properties of all joints studied.The student will determine the need for and implement methods of re-evaluation, including various outcome measures, of the treatment, plan, and goals.The student will identify and promote the health needs of individuals, groups and communities including joint care and the prevention of deformities subsequent to problems such as rheumatoid arthritis and osteoarthritis.The student will incorporate an algorithmic approach (which infers differential diagnosis) in order to evaluate the patient’s problems leading to the PT diagnosis, classification, and prognosis.The student will perform an age appropriate orthopedic examination to include history, posture, pain, muscle function, range of motion, joint play, ligamentous integrity, neurological testing, palpatory evaluation, biomechanical analysis, & function.The student will recognize when to refer to other physical therapists and members of the health care team when indicated.The student will synthesize the results from the examination to determine the nature of the patient’s problem, and prioritize the primary problems affecting the patient.Using clinical judgment and reflection to enhance clinical reasoning and patient outcomes, the student will safely perform physical therapy intervention to include mobilization techniques, modalities, exercise programs, and home programs.

course_name: Foundations of Orthopedics for the Upper Quarter in Physical Therapy
description: This course emphasizes the evaluation and treatment of common musculoskeletal problems of the shoulder, elbow, wrist, and hand.  The course is designed around the understanding of and subsequent application to case studies of the anatomy, mechanics, pathomechanics, pathology, surgical intervention, and rehabilitation involving the upper quarter using an evidenced-based approach.   Requisites: PT 7701 and PT 7702   Repeat/Retake Information: May not be retaken.  Lecture/Lab Hours: 2.0 lecture  Grades: Eligible Grades: A-F,PR,WP,WF,WN,FN,AU,I  Learning Outcomes:  The student will be able to identify the signs, symptoms, pain patterns, mechanism of injury and surgical repair of selected upper extremity musculoskeletal conditions.The student will be able to analyze upper extremity musculoskeletal conditions to determine clusters of signs and symptoms, etiology, mechanism of injury, appropriate surgical procedures, resultant movement dysfunctions, and the prognosis for recovery.The student will be able to apply relevant biological and biomechanical characteristics of upper extremity tissues to functional and clinical situations.The student will be able to analyze the impact of normal and abnormal movement patterns, muscle flexibility/strength, and capsule properties on the function of the upper quarter.The student will be able to determine patient/client goals and outcomes within available resources and specify the prognosis including expected length of time to achieve the goals and outcomes based on current evidence.The student will be able to establish a safe, effective, realistic, culturally competent, and patient centered plan of care that addresses the interests of the patient and family members, payers, other professionals and other appropriate individuals.The student will be able to apply and integrate current knowledge, theory, and professional judgment while considering the patient/client perspective, the environment, and available resources.The student will be able to access and critically analyze scientific literature and other sources of information related to physical therapy practice and research and integrate with clinical judgement to determine the best care for a client.The student will be able to identify red flag items related to patients/clients presenting with upper extremity pain and dysfunction.

course_name: Clinical Applications for the Upper Quarter in Physical Therapy
description: This course emphasizes the development of clinical evaluation and treatment skills used by the physical therapist in the care of clients with musculoskeletal problems of the shoulder, elbow, wrist and hand. Critical thinking and differential diagnosis skills are developed in conjunction with the assessment and treatment process. Evaluation and treatment are presented in the context of the contemporary healthcare and reimbursement systems   Requisites: PT 7701 and PT 7702   Repeat/Retake Information: May not be retaken. administer upper quarter tests and measures appropriate to the patient’s age, diagnosis and health status, based on the patient/client’s presentation and cultural background.Students will be able to identify clients with red flag signs and symptoms.Students will be able to demonstrate an algorithmic assessment scheme that is guided by patient/client’s signs, symptoms, responses, and movement when reasoning to minimize errors and enhance patient/client outcomes.The student will be able to formulate a physical therapy prognosis based on the patient/client’s presentation and evaluation outcomes.The student will be able to determine those components of the plan of care that may, or may not, be directed to the physical therapist assistant.The student will be able to demonstrate effective and efficient treatment techniques for the patient/client with upper extremity pain and dysfunction which achieve the patient/client goals and outcomes.The student will be able to determine when it is appropriate to terminate a physical therapy plan of care.The student will be able to access and critically analyze scientific literature and other sources of information related to physical therapy practice and research and integrate with clinical judgement to determine the best care for a client.

course_name: Foundations of Orthopedics for the Lower Quarter
description:
This course focuses on the physical therapy evaluation and treatment of lower extremity conditions (hip, knee, lower leg, ankle, and foot)  from an evidence-based perspective. Conservative approaches, surgical, and non-traditional approaches to lower extremity
assessment and care will be discussed.   Requisites: PT 7041 and 7042   Repeat/Retake Information: May not be retaken.  Lecture/Lab Hours: 2.0 lecture  Grades: Eligible Grades: A-F,PR,WP,WF,WN,FN,AU,I  Learning Outcomes:  The student will be able to identify physiologic and pathologic pain and the effects on evaluation and treatment in the orthopedic patient.The student will be able to examine selected conditions in terms of etiology, mechanism of injury, surgery, signs and symptoms, resultant deformities, and prognosis for recovery, based on biological/biomechanical characteristics of leg tissues.The student will be able to analyze the impact of normal and abnormal movement, muscle flexibility/strength, and capsule properties on the function of the lower extremity..The student will be able to develop and manage a physical therapy plan of care that is safe, effective, and patient/client centered, and based upon current clinical guidelines.The student will be able to determine patient/client goals and outcomes within available resources and specify expected length of time to achieve the goals and outcomes based on current evidence.The student will be able to integrate the best evidence for practice from sources of information with clinical judgment and patient/client values to determine the best care for a patient/client.The student will be able to critically evaluate sources of information related to physical therapy practice and research and apply knowledge from these sources in a scientific manner and to appropriate populations.The student will be able to identify red flag items related to patients/clients presenting with lower extremity pain and dysfunction including that of direct access or independent practice setting.The student will be able to demonstrate knowledge of the efficacy of taping and bracing for the lower extremity patient.

course_name: Clinical Applications for the Lower Quarter
description:
This course emphasizes the development of clinical evaluation and treatment skills used by the physical therapist in the care of clients with
lower extremity pain and dysfunction. Regional areas of emphasis include the hip, knee, lower leg, ankle, and foot. Critical thinking and differential diagnosis skills are developed in conjunction with the assessment and treatment process. Evaluation and treatment are presented in the context of the contemporary healthcare and reimbursement systems.   Requisites: PT 7041 and 7042   Repeat/Retake Information: May not be retaken. Focuses on the orthopedic examination and treatment of the spine for physical therapists.  Manual skills and appropriate exercise programs for the spine will be developed. course_name: Foundations of Orthopedics for the Spine
description: This course focuses on the physical therapy evaluation and treatment of spinal conditions (SIJ, lumbar, thoracic, and cervical) as well as TMJ dysfunction from an evidence-based perspective. Conservative approaches, surgical, and non-traditional approaches to spinal assessment and care will be discussed.   Requisites: PT 7721 and PT 7722   Repeat/Retake Information: May not be retaken. This course emphasizes the development of clinical evaluation and treatment skills used by the physical therapist in the care of clients with spinal pain (sacroiliac joint, lumbar, thoracic, and cervical) or jaw dysfunction. Critical thinking and differential diagnosis skills are developed in conjunction with the assessment and treatment process. course_name: Planning and Implementing a Physical Therapy Service
description: Provides basic knowledge and skills needed to plan and implement a physical therapy service. course_name: Management, Leadership, and Ethical and Legal Practice in Physical Therapy
description: Topics include management styles, negotiation, licensing of health professionals, the state practice act, the American Physical Therapy Association (APTA), the Federation of State Boards of Physical Therapy (FSBPT), leadership definition and experiential learning in professional leadership, and analysis of conetemporary issues in physical therapy practice. Lecture/Lab Hours: 5.0 lecture  Grades: Eligible Grades: A-F,PR,WP,WF,WN,FN,AU,I  Learning Outcomes:  Delineate and understand the role of a licensing board in practice management, in public safety, and in the life of a practicing therapist.The student will acquire an appreciation of the function of the APTA and value the website for apta.org as a resource.The student will analyze and apply the and the process for becoming involved in leadership activities.The student will identify and discuss various practice issues that concern the profession today.The student will identify ethical and legal obligations of the physical therapist to the patient, to the employer, to the profession, and to society.The student will participate in leadership opportunities within the state of Ohio and/or nationally, including the state board and the OPTA.The student will participate in legislative issues relating to patient advocacy and the practice of physical therapy through knowledge of issues and bills related to the same and communicating directly with legislators on appropriate issues.The student will select appropriate resources for gaining information about professional issues.The student will understand the role of the Federation of State Boards in the practice of physical therapy.

course_name: Synthesis of Professional Development in Physical Therapy
description: This course is designed to engage students at the culmination of their professional development as a student physical therapist.  This course covers current select professional, legal, and ethical issues in physical therapy practice.  Students will reflect and discuss their various professional and service-learning experiences throughout the physical therapy curriculum and the impact of these on their own professional development.  Additionally, career planning and lifelong professional planning are approached through the completion of their professional portfolio.   Requisites: PT 8330   Repeat/Retake Information: May not be retaken.  Lecture/Lab Hours: 2.0 lecture  Grades: Eligible Grades: A-F,PR,WP,WF,WN,FN,AU,I  Learning Outcomes:  The student will be able to justify the legal and ethical obligations of the physical therapist to patients, to employers, to the profession, and to society.The student will be able to analyze the main elements of laws that are of particular relevance to physical therapists including but not limited to the following: negligence, malpractice, fraud, assault and battery, sexual harassment and sexual misconduct.The student will be able to explain concepts of risk management.The student will be able to analyze and apply the Ohio Revised Code regarding the licensing of physical therapists.The student will be able to summarize the local laws regarding supervision of physical therapist assistants and physical therapy and physical therapy assistant students.The student will be able to explain the Realm-Individual Process-Situation model of ethical decision making and use it along with American Physical Therapy Association Code of Ethics to justify a response to an ethical dilemma.The student will be able to conclude and defend possible licensure action to be taken by the Ohio PT Board based on a situation discussed at an attended Ohio PT Board Meetng.The student will be able to compare and contrast effective vs ineffective communication.The student will be able to design a job seeking strategy to include identification of available positions, resume and cover letter writing, and intervieweing techniques.The student will be able to appraise the function and processes of the Ohio Physical Therapy Association and the American Physical Therapy Association.The student will be able to compose and support a motion in a Mock House of Delegates to appraise the value of policy development in the American Physical Therapy Association.The student will be able to describe the relevance of the Federation of State Boards of Physical Therapy (FSBPT).

course_name: Physical Therapy Management of Pediatric Disorders
description: Students acquire knowledge in the assessment and management of children with selected neuromuscular and musculoskeletal problems that arise in infancy and childhood.  Designed to provide student physical therapists with a variety of learning experiences emphasizing clinical knowledge and skills that underlie effective provision of professional services for infants, children, and adolescents. available to the pediatric client including early intervention services, educational resources, Children Services, etc.Students will describe the unique sociologic, economic, and cultural implications with practice management of the pediatric patient/client.Students will design functional activities for children, teachers, and parents to use outside the therapeutic environment that are consistent with expected outcomes, available resources, and the family environment and needs.Students will differentiate between functional (typical) and dysfunctional (atypical) adaptive responses of the developing individual based.Students will discuss the optimal uses and limitations of various developmental screening and evaluation tools.Students will examine pediatric patient/client’s neuromotor development by choosing and correctly administering the Alberta Infant Motor Scale (AIMS) or Peabody Developmental Motor Scales (PDMS-2) in a laboratory setting.Students will explain the importance of collaboration and communication with family, caregivers, teachers, other health care professionals to maximize outcomes of PT interventions and reduce/prevent secondary impairments or future disabilities.Students will explain the role of the physical therapist in the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit, within Early Intervention and school settings, and other therapeutic settings.Students will explain the theories, principles and stages of typical development for balance, postural alignment and gross motor skills.Students will identify red flags and contraindications for interventions based on assessment findings, patient/client diagnosis and most current evidence.Students will list risk reduction strategies including positioning instructions, adaptive equipment, bracing, seating and other assistive devices that may be indicated for patients/clients to reduce/prevent secondary impairments.Students will monitor children’s emotional and physical response to assessment and intervention procedures and adjust accordingly.Students will produce accurate and professional documentation utilizing developmental evaluation instruments.Students will promote and sustain ethical and culturally appropriate professional relationships with colleagues, children and families.Students will recognize risk factors in order to promote prevention of pediatric conditions such as patients/clients/typical children in the laboratory and clinic.Students will use knowledge of relationships among areas of the musculoskeletal and central nervous systems, disease processes and motor development to explain clinically discernible orthopedic dysfunction and provide a rationale for intervention.Students will utilize play and peer interaction in intervention development, explaining its importance with the pediatric population.Using the laboratory assessments and case based scenarios, students will determine physical therapy diagnosis, interventions, short and long term goals, prognosis, equipment recommendations, and discharge plans for pediatric clients.

positioning instructions, adaptive equipment, bracing, seating and other devices indicated for clients with atypical neuromuscular development to reduce secondary impairments.The student will be able to promote prevention of various pediatric conditions such as apophysitis, sports injuries, chronic pain, childhood obesity, etc through recognition and identification of the risk factors student will be able to modify plan of service appropriately based on children’s emotional and physiological response to assessment and intervention procedures.The student will be able to appraise the value of outcome measurements for maximizing physical therapy interventions with the pediatric population.The student will be able to select appropriate Sensory Integration principles that can be incorporated into assessment, evaluation, diagnosis and intervention of pediatric clients in case-based scenario(s).The student will be able to explain the importance of collaboration and communication with family, caregivers, teachers, other health care professionals, etc. to foster a family-centered and interdisciplinary model of care.The student will be able to summarize services beyond physical therapy that are typically available to the pediatric client including early intervention services, educational resources, Children Services, etc.The student will be able to conclude when there is child/family need for referral to other services and explain the professional responsibility of the clinician.The student will be able to compare and contrast the role(s) of the physical therapist in the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit, within Early Intervention and school settings, and other therapeutic settings.The student will be able to select and justify appropriate pediatric interventions to be delegated to the physical therapist assistant.The student will be able to promote and sustain ethical and culturally appropriate professional relationships with colleagues, children and families.The student will be able to discuss the unique sociologic, economic and cultural implications for practice management of the pediatric patient/client.

course_name: College Mathematics Teaching for New Teaching Assistants
description: This course prepares new mathematics teaching assistants for undergraduate-level mathematics instruction. Key math content topics such as algebra, calculus, discrete mathematics, and mathematical modeling, studied throughout the AYA Math Content courses are revisited in light of their applicability to High School mathematics. Business analytics can be subcategorized into three primary fields of study. These fields include descriptive, predictive, and prescriptive analytics. The course provides students with a deeper understanding of corporate finance. In short, students will be able to address key company specific questions about the firm’s strategy and ability to fund its operations, while at the same time managing and incorporating risk management to maximize shareholder wealth. course_name: World of Late Antiquity: Culture and Society in the Late Roman Empire
description: Beginning in the third century, the mighty Roman Empire began its slow but inevitable decline and fall, brought to a decisive end by the barbarian invasions of the late fourth and fifth century, epitomized by the sack of Rome by Goths in 410 and Vandals in 455, and terminated with the deposition of the last western emperor in 476. That is one vision of the period sometimes called Late Antiquity. The other vision sees the transformation of classical culture, closely related to the emergence of Christianity, and diverse political and social changes that would live on long after the imperial political order disappeared in the west. This course will take account of both these visions, with a strong preference for continuity over decline. Readings and lectures will explore important aspects of political, intellectual, religious, and social change. Discussions and written assignments will depend on the interpretation of primary sources, including a wide variety of literary and material evidence. The course is a bridge between the courses on the Roman Empire and Barbarian West, but students are not expected to have taken either course. It challenges students to understand capitalism less as a hegemonic, clearly-defined force, but rather as a multi-faceted concept that has, throughout history and in our own time, informed the beliefs and actions of monarchy and leaders, philosophers, economists, producers, consumers, and citizens. course_name: Learning and Teaching World History for Graduate Students
description: World History is a comparatively new, or at least newly redefined and newly important, field of teaching, research, and writing in our discipline. Many history graduate students have never studied it, or have been introduced to it only in cursory or piecemeal fashion, yet are increasingly called upon to refer to it, utilize its findings and insights in their own work, and … teach it. One obvious goal is to provide a quick and broad-brushed overview of the basic content of World History. Covers major periods in world history from the beginning to the present, highlighting major global changes and their interconnectness. A second goal is to develop a sensitivity to and critical sense about such fundamental matters as structure, generalization, and perspective in World History. Considerable time is spent discussing these, and emphasizing areas in which comparative study is and is not appropriate. A third goal is to introduce some of the major themes and issues that attract debate among world historians these days, and to appreciate the strengths and weaknesses which they pose. This attention to current historiography, especially in a new field, is critical for showing the differences and similarities between today’s World History and other perspectives on the study of the past. Along the way, we will consider some strategies for coming to terms with the welter of information and opinion in this often unwieldy field, and for approaching it in ways that are useful to learning and understanding what it has to offer to the study of other varieties of history. A final aim is to introduce graduate students to the many challenges and approaches to teaching this subject. The intent is not only to prepare graduate students for teaching their own World History surveys, but to suggest ways in which they can incorporate global perspectives into their own scholarship and into a variety of possible teaching assignments. Students follow common readings and individual readings, and produce weekly papers on these readings, which are discussed intensively in a seminar setting. The final portion is devoted to students producing an original syllabus for an undergraduate course in World History (either Before 1750 or Since 1750), of sufficient quality to be used in the classroom. This intended to better prepare our graduates to enter the real teaching world of today, in which most will be asked at one time another to talk about and teach World History, and in which having taken a course like this can be a critical factor in an academic job interview.   Requisites:   Repeat/Retake Information: May not be retaken.  Lecture/Lab Hours: 4.0 seminar  Grades: Eligible Grades: A-F,PR,WP,WF,WN,FN,AU,I  Learning Outcomes:  Acquaintance with the basic themes and periods and information in World History.Acquaintance with the major approaches and challenges inherent in teach World History.Acquaintance with the major themes and issues that attract debate among world historians these days, and to appreciate the strengths and weaknesses which they pose.Acquire a sensitivity to and critical sense about such fundamental matters as structure, generalization, and perspective in World History.Completion of a classroom-ready syllabus in World History, either pre-1750 or since 1750.

Introduces the concepts relevant to the acutely/critically ill adult client at the level of the acute care nurse practitioner. Addresses nurse practitioner/patient relationship, clinical management, health care delivery, and professional responsibility. Focuses on review and development of tools used in assessing the family system and its impact on individual members. Design of family-based interventions is emphasized.   Requisites: NRSE 6020 and 6230   Repeat/Retake Information: May be repeated for a maximum of 6.0 hours. course_name: Neurobiological and Theoretical Bases for Psychiatric Mental Health in Advanced Nursing Practice
description: This course examines the neurobiological and theoretical bases as they apply to advanced nursing practice in psychiatric mental health throughout the life span. This course builds on the fundamental knowledge of anatomy, physiology, pathophysiology, and psychology. The material presented in this course reflects the current knowledge of neurobiology and the theoretical bases for the clinical manifestations of psychiatric mental health disorders throughout the lifespan.   Requisites: Student in online Post-Masters Psychiatric Nurse Practitioner (PMHNP) program   Repeat/Retake Information: May not be retaken.  Lecture/Lab Hours: 3.0 lecture  Grades: Eligible Grades: A-F,WP,WF,WN,FN,AU,I  Learning Outcomes:  Students will be able to explain the brain structure, function, and influence on the development of psychiatric mental health disorders.Students will be able to identify theory and evidence-based interventions to advanced practice with psychiatric mental health disorders.Students will be able to explain the role of co-morbid conditions or symptoms of select psychiatric mental health disorders throughout the life span.Students will be able to compare and contrast select theoretical models and their applications to advanced practice nursing in psychiatric mental health.Students will be able to appraise the role of genetics and epigenetics in the development and management of select psychiatric mental health disorders.Students will be able to apply the concepts of mind-body connections in the symptomatology and management of select mental health disorders.

course_name: Psychotherapeutic Treatment Modalities for Advanced Nursing Practice
description: This course presents the nonpharmacological treatment modalities for psychiatric mental health disorders throughout the lifespan. A variety of conceptual models and treatment modalities are introduced to the student. Evidence based therapy models for groups, families and individuals are emphasized. Lecture/Lab Hours: 3.0 lecture  Grades: Eligible Grades: A-F,WP,WF,WN,FN,AU,I  Learning Outcomes:  Students will be able to compare and contrast psychotherapeutic modalities that are appropriate for selected psychiatric mental health disorders throughout the lifespan.Students will be able to demonstrative communication techniques and strategies used with psychotherapeutic modalities.Students will be able to explain the core competencies for psychotherapy for the advanced practice psychiatric mental health nurse.Students will be able to explain the role of the advanced practice psychiatric mental health nurse in the development and implementation of a treatment plan that includes psychotherapeutic modalities.

course_name: Assessment & Management of Mental Health Disorders for Advanced Nursing Practice I
description: This is the first of two courses encompassing advanced health assessment techniques for diagnosis and management of mental health disorders throughout the lifespan. Included is development of differential diagnosis, planning, and evaluation of care using psychotherapeutic modalities, psychopharmacology, and community resources. Addresses the influence of family dynamics as well as societal influences on mental health and recovery. The concepts of both acute and chronic treatment as they apply to disorders of mood, neurodevelopment, sleep, anxiety, and other select disorders are discussed. Lecture/Lab Hours: 3.0 lecture  Grades: Eligible Grades: A-F,WP,WF,WN,FN,AU,I  Learning Outcomes:  Students will be able to analyze the interdisciplinary approach to care for the mental health patient provided by the advanced practice nurse and other providers.Students will be able to demonstrate beginning clinical competence in the recognition, assessment, and management of selected psychiatric mental health disorders throughout the lifespan.Students will be able to demonstrate selection of appropriate, evidence based treatment modalities including psychotherapy, psychopharmacology, complementary, and alternative treatment for selected mental health disorders throughout the lifespan.Students will be able to evaluate interventions and outcomes in advanced practice nursing with the psychiatric mental health patient.Students will be able to utilize critical thinking skills in advanced assessment, management, and planning of care for patients throughout the lifespan with psychiatric mental health disorders.

course_name: Assessment and Management of Mental Health Disorders for Advanced Nursing Practice II
description: This is the second of two courses encompassing advanced assessment techniques for the diagnosis and management of psychiatric mental health disorders throughout the lifespan. Included is the development of differential diagnoses, planning, and evaluation of care using psychotherapeutic modalities, psychopharmacology, and community resources. Addresses the influences of family dynamics as well as societal influences on mental health and recovery. Lecture/Lab Hours: 3.0 lecture  Grades: Eligible Grades: A-F,WP,WF,WN,FN,AU,I  Learning Outcomes:  Students will be able to analyze the interdisciplinary approach to care for the psychiatric mental health patient provided by the advanced practice nurse and other providers.Students will be able to demonstrate clinical competence in the recognition, assessment, and management of selected psychiatric mental health disorders throughout the lifespan.Students will be able to demonstrate critical thinking skills in advanced assessment, management, and planning of care for patients with psychiatric mental health disorders throughout the lifespan.Students will be able to evaluate and revise interventions and outcomes in advanced practice nursing with the psychiatric mental health patient.Students will be to demonstrate selection of appropriate, evidence based treatment modalities including psychotherapy, psychopharmacology, complementary and alternative treatment for psychiatric mental health disorders throughout the lifespan.

Focuses on theory and strategies of curriculum design. Emphasizes application of principles to the design of an educational curriculum.   Requisites: NRSE 6010 and 7802   Repeat/Retake Information: May be repeated for a maximum of 6.0 hours.  Lecture/Lab Hours: 3.0 lecture  Grades: Eligible Grades: A-F,WP,WF,WN,FN,AU,I  Learning Outcomes:  Students will be able to apply curriculum development guidelines to the design of an educational program.Students will be able to compare and contrast curricula developed for professional and client populations.Students will be able to examine theories and strategies of curriculum development.Students will be able to explore the development of the various components of nursing education.

Focuses on enhancing understanding of the academic faculty role with an emphasis on program evaluation responsibilities.   Requisites: NRSE 6620   Repeat/Retake Information: May be repeated for a maximum of 6.0 hours. Addresses roles and responsibilities of the nurse administrator. Provides the opportunity to analyze critical attributes, knowledge, and skills required in the administration of health care settings.   Requisites: NRSE 6010 and (6110 ro 602) and 6120   Repeat/Retake Information: May be repeated for a maximum of 6.0 hours. This course focuses on application of advanced assessment, diagnostic, and intervention skills in a clinical practice environment for nurse practitioners. The focus of this course is on synthesis of theory and implementation of the role of the adult-gerontology acute care nurse practitioner (AGACNP) for post-master’s certificate students. course_name: Leadership in Systems and Organizations for Advanced Nursing Practice
description: This course focuses on tranformational leadership, leadership theories and a systems perspective including complexity theory. course_name: Health Policy and Advocacy for Advanced Nursing Practice
description: This course focuses on integration and understanding of healthcare policy and advocacy.  An analysis of the process for influencing a health policy agenda is examined. course_name: Principles of Business and Resource Management for Advanced Nursing Practice
description: The course focuses on the principles of business, strategic planning, entrepreneurship and financial implications in advanced nursing practice. course_name: Analysis of Evidence-based Practice for Advanced Nursing Practice
description: The course focuses on critical appraisal, synthesis of healthcare research, and evaluation of literature to inform evidence-based practice and develop a clinically relevant question. The course focuses on the impact of informatics used by advanced practice nurses to promote quality healthcare. course_name: Primary Care of Adults and Older Adults

Effort will be placed on developing proficiencies in a range of skills required to practice consulting as well as start, scale and run a successful organization. The course is relevant to those 1) who are specifically interested in consulting careers and / or 2) whose area of interest involves entrepreneurship, starting, scaling, managing and leading organizations in the public/non-profit sectors.   Requisites:   Repeat/Retake Information: May not be retaken.  Lecture/Lab Hours: 3.0 seminar  Grades: Eligible Grades: A-F,CR,PR,WP,WF,WN,FN,AU,I  Learning Outcomes:  Develop strategies and recommendations for entrepreneurial issues.Gain knowledge of consulting practices.Gain practice in conducting a field-consulting project.Improve your ability to define key factors and issues relevant to a consulting engagement and examine their inter-relationships and learn to “massage” them conceptually.Improve your ability to present analyses of entrepreneurial and organizational issues and problems in a concise, accurate, clear and interesting manner from the perspective of a consultant.

Entrepreneurship education, in the sense of focusing on the creation of new economic entities centered
on a novel product/service, has been, until recently, relatively rare. At Ohio University, a pedagogy has
been developed focused on inter-disciplinary team-based projects that result in new venture formation and
long-term success for the newly-founded companies and the University that developed the research and
technologies which are the basis for many of the companies. The curriculum is structured such that
students from the disciplines of science, medicine, engineering, communication, and business can be
engaged and participate.   Requisites:   Repeat/Retake Information: May not be retaken.  Lecture/Lab Hours: 3.0 seminar  Grades: Eligible Grades: A-F,CR,PR,WP,WF,WN,FN,AU,I  Learning Outcomes:  Acquire skills and techniques necessary for the creation and development of successful entrepreneurship in technological fields.Know how to recognize opportunities, assess technologies and markets, and execute commercialization analysis.Understand the world of technology entrepreneurship.

Culture-based approach to increased language proficiency designed to foster openness toward, empathy for, and curiosity about Malaysian speakers. Students continue to develop listening, reading, speaking, and writing skills as they study the diverse history and customs of Malaysian speakers.
